question: What does Article IX say about the Superintendent of Public Instruction?
answer:
- The Superintendent of Public Instruction is elected by the qualified electors of the State at each gubernatorial election. The Superintendent takes office on the first Monday after the first day of January following the gubernatorial election and may not serve more than two terms [1].
- On the Superintendent’s nomination, the State Board of Education shall appoint one Deputy Superintendent and three Associate Superintendents, who are exempt from state civil service and serve four-year terms. Additional Associate Superintendents may be appointed in accordance with law but are subject to state civil service [1].

question: How does Title 1 describe county board or county superintendent responsibilities?
answer:
Summary of responsibilities described in Title 1 for county boards of education and county superintendents, based on the provided excerpts:

County board of education
- Adopt rules and regulations governing administration of the county superintendent’s office [3].
- Review, revise, and approve the county superintendent’s annual itemized estimate of anticipated revenues and expenditures before it is filed with the auditor; it cannot be filed or approved by the board of supervisors until the county board has reviewed and approved it [3].
- Acquire, lease, lease‑purchase, hold, and convey real property to house the offices and services of the county superintendent, but only for county boards to which the relevant duties of the county board of supervisors under Section 1080(b) have been transferred (excluding recreational duties) [3].
- Contract for and employ specialized services (financial, economic, accounting, engineering, legal, administrative) and pay appropriate compensation from available funds [3].
- Fill by appointment any vacancy in the office of the county superintendent of schools; in counties with an elected superintendent, the appointee serves until the office is filled at the next gubernatorial election. This appointment authority vests only if adopted by the board at a public meeting under Article 1 (commencing with Section 1000) [2].
- Receive, upon a consenting resolution by the county board of supervisors, the transfer of specified functions (including receipt of petitions, reports, and other papers under enumerated sections); thereafter, references to the “board of supervisors” in those sections are deemed to refer to the county board of education [2].
- Enter agreements with school district and community college district governing boards for centralized in‑service training programs for certificated and classified employees under the direction of the county superintendent’s office; these programs are financed through the county school service fund and included in the budget under Article 3 (commencing with Section 14050) of Part 9 [5].
- The county board president may appoint members of the county board to serve on a school district or community college district governing board when vacancies exist in a majority of that board’s offices, until new members are elected or appointed [6].
- Establish the administrative duties of an administrative adviser, who counsels with and coordinates among the district attorney or county counsel, the county board of education, the county committee on school district organization, the personnel commission, the county superintendent, and districts requesting services [4].

County superintendent of schools
- Prepare and maintain in the superintendent’s office a record of all actions taken by the county committee on school district organization regarding trustee area boundaries [1].
- Prescribe the duties of a supervisor of health employed by the superintendent for supervision of pupil health [4].
- Award consultancy contracts to retired certificated employees of the superintendent’s office or of a district or community college district in the county who served at least 10 years and are at least 55 years of age [4].
- With county board approval, provide advisory services in school business administration, maintenance of school buildings and grounds, and processing of credential-related issues as designated by the State Department of Education [5].

question: How does Title 1 describe county board or county superintendent responsibilities?
answer:
County board of education responsibilities (Title 1):
- Adopt rules and regulations governing administration of the county superintendent’s office [3].
- Review and approve the county superintendent’s annual itemized estimate of anticipated revenues and expenditures before it is filed with the auditor or approved by the board of supervisors; the board may make revisions, reductions, or additions it deems proper [3].
- Acquire, lease, lease-purchase, hold, and convey real property to house the county superintendent’s offices and services, where those duties have been transferred from the board of supervisors under Education Code Section 1080 (excluding certain recreational functions) [3].
- Contract for special services and advice (financial, economic, accounting, engineering, legal, or administrative) and pay appropriate compensation [3].
- Fill, by appointment, any vacancy in the office of the county superintendent (in counties where the superintendent is elected), with the appointee serving until the office is filled at the next gubernatorial election; this authority applies only if adopted by the county board at a public meeting pursuant to Section 1000 [2].
- Assume specified functions otherwise performed by the county board of supervisors (e.g., receipt of petitions, reports, and other papers under listed Education Code sections) if the board of supervisors adopts a resolution consenting to transfer; after transfer, references to the board of supervisors in those sections mean the county board of education [2].
- Establish the administrative duties of an administrative adviser who coordinates among the district attorney or county counsel, the county board, the county committee on school district organization, the personnel commission, the county superintendent, and school and community college districts requesting services [4].
- Enter agreements with school district and community college district governing boards for centralized in‑service training programs under the direction of the county superintendent’s office; these programs are financed through the county school service fund and included in the county office budget [5].
- If a majority of seats on a school district or community college district governing board become vacant, the president of the county board may appoint county board members to that governing board until new members are elected or appointed [6].

County superintendent of schools responsibilities (Title 1):
- Prepare and keep a record, in the superintendent’s office, of all actions taken by the county committee on school district organization related to trustee area boundaries [1].
- Prescribe the duties of the supervisor of health, who performs duties related to supervising pupil health as directed by the superintendent [4].
- Award consultancy contracts to retired certificated employees of the county office or districts in the county who served at least 10 years and are at least 55 years of age [4].
- With county board approval, provide advisory services in school business administration, maintenance of school buildings and grounds, and processing credential-related problems as designated by the State Department of Education [5].
- Direct the centralized in‑service training programs conducted under agreements with district and community college governing boards [5].

question: What does Title 1 say about coordination between state and local education bodies?
answer:
- Policy direction: Through the Compact for Education, Title 1 encourages “close cooperation and understanding” among executive, legislative, professional, and lay leadership “on a nationwide basis at the state and local levels,” provides a forum and clearinghouse to share solutions, seeks to “facilitate the improvement of state and local educational systems,” and expressly encourages both local and state initiative while respecting diversity among localities and states [4][2].

- County–district coordination: Title 1 authorizes county superintendents to provide in-service programs and “coordinative services” to school and community college district governing boards, and, upon request, to provide consultative or coordinative services for federally funded local programs (with those services eligible for federal financing) [5]. Services that are not inter-district coordination must be delivered in ways that strengthen districts and respect the Legislature’s grant of responsibility to districts “to determine and administer their own educational program.” County superintendents may cooperatively provide services across county lines when that is more economical and effective, and their direct operation of educational programs is limited to emergencies where students would otherwise be denied education. Services may include those “which relate to the coordination of the educational program or coordination of the course of study among districts under [the superintendent’s] jurisdiction” [3].

- Financial responsibility in coordinated arrangements: Local educational agencies may not use participation in a joint powers authority to avoid legal obligations or state financial obligations, nor to shift costs or liability to the state unless a state entity is a party to the agreement and expressly agrees. LEAs retain ultimate responsibility if a joint powers authority defaults [1].

question: What does Title 1 say about coordination between state and local education bodies?
answer:
Title 1 addresses coordination chiefly in three ways:

- State–local policy coordination (Compact for Education): It establishes a forum and clearinghouse to promote close cooperation among executive, legislative, professional, and lay education leaders at both state and local levels; encourages local and state initiative; and aims to improve state and local educational systems while respecting diversity among localities and states [4][2].

- County–district coordination within California: County superintendents provide services to school and community college districts in ways that recognize district responsibility to determine and administer their own programs; services should strengthen—not supplant—district capacity; two or more county superintendents may cooperatively provide services across county lines when economical and effective; and direct county operation of educational programs is limited to emergencies. County superintendent services under this chapter may include coordination of educational programs and courses of study among districts under their jurisdiction [3].

- Coordinative and consultative services: County superintendents may offer in-service and coordinative services to district governing boards, and upon request may provide consultative/coordinative services for federally funded programs in districts within their jurisdiction [5].

Additionally, financial coordination limits: local education agencies may not use joint powers authorities to avoid legal or financial obligations to the state or shift costs to the state unless the state is a party and expressly agrees; locals retain ultimate responsibility, including if a joint powers authority defaults [1].

question: Does Title 1 include exceptions or carve-outs to general administrative requirements?
answer:
Yes. Title 1 includes several provisions that function as exceptions or special rules modifying otherwise general administrative requirements. Examples include:

- Expanded disciplinary grounds beyond general civil service rules: While designated positions are subject to Government Code Article 2 (starting with § 19590), the board may also take action for additional fiduciary-related causes not otherwise specified in that article—an augmentation to the ordinary civil service framework [2].

- Apportionment adjustments in reorganization: When annexation or inclusion of a district occurs before a conditional apportionment, the board may reconsider applications, withhold or make conditional apportionments as necessary, rather than follow the ordinary apportionment path [5].

question: What duties in Title 1 are mandatory versus discretionary?
answer:
Below are mandatory (shall) versus discretionary (may/authorized) duties reflected in the provided Title 1 excerpts.

Mandatory duties (shall):
- A board must:
  - Establish eligibility qualifications for district apportionments under the chapter [3].
  - Establish procedures and policies for administering the chapter and expending funds [3].
  - Adopt rules and regulations for administering the chapter, including required procedures, forms, and information [3].
  - Prescribe instructions for disposing of property being replaced through an apportionment; affected school districts must comply, and compliance is a condition of the apportionment [3].
  - Dispose of replaced property (if title is transferred) in a manner it deems appropriate to ensure the highest return to the state [3].
- Affected school districts must comply with the board’s property-disposition instructions [3].
- The authority’s governance:
  - Two members constitute a quorum; a majority of a quorum is necessary for action; vacancies do not impair the authority’s ability to perform its duties; meetings must be open to the public and comply with the Government Code’s open-meeting provisions [4].
  - The chapter must be administered by the authority, which is vested with all powers reasonably necessary to carry out its granted or imposed responsibilities [4].
- The retirement board must regulate duties of employers, employing agencies, and other public authorities imposed by the part, and must require reports from them [5].
- Post-employment restriction: specified former officials shall not, for two years after leaving their positions, represent others for compensation before the board to influence actions listed in the statute [5].
- Interpretive/structural rules:
  - Unless otherwise provided, general provisions govern construction of the code [6].
  - Joint authority given to three or more officers is exercised by a majority, unless otherwise expressed [6].

Discretionary duties/powers (may/authorized to):
- Property and apportionment:
  - The board may require a district to transfer title to replaced property to the state; after transfer, the board determines how to dispose of it to ensure the highest return [3].
- Authority operations:
  - The authority may delegate powers and duties to members or its executive director [4].
  - The authority is authorized to adopt bylaws, adopt an official seal, sue and be sued, and receive and accept gifts, grants, or donations from specified public entities [4].
- Retirement board:
  - The board may take disciplinary action for causes related to fiduciary responsibility, in addition to other specified causes [5].
- Grants and trustees:
  - A grantor may provide additional terms necessary to carry out the grant’s purpose, including specifying trades/professions to be taught and terms for admitting deserving scholars; a grantor may also provide for maintaining free scholarships for specified classes of children [1].
  - Rules prescribed by a grantor for managing conveyed property are, unless otherwise prescribed by the grantor, deemed advisory only and do not preclude trustees from making changes as conditions require (i.e., trustees retain discretion) [1].
- Delegation of public duties generally:
  - When a power is granted to, or a duty imposed upon, a public officer, it may be exercised or performed by a deputy or by a person authorized by the officer, unless the code expressly provides otherwise [6].

Notes:
- The above identifies mandatory versus discretionary duties only from the provided Title 1 passages and is not exhaustive of all Title 1 provisions. Sources: [1], [3], [4], [5], [6].

question: What does Title 1 say about publication or transparency of education information?
answer:
Based on the provided excerpts from Title 1, the code addresses publication and transparency in these ways:

- County superintendent publications: The State Board of Education must establish definitions for “publications,” and each county superintendent of schools, upon making any publication, must transmit a copy to the State Board of Education. Additionally, once a county superintendent’s budget is approved by the Superintendent of Public Instruction, a copy is transmitted to the county superintendent and to the county auditor. [3]

- Financial transparency and accountability: Title 1 establishes a program of financial and compliance audits for school districts and county superintendents’ offices to promote accountability over public educational funding, with the Controller having primary oversight. These audits are to meet federal single-audit requirements and verify that funds are expended as required by law or regulation. [4]

- Public posting of Title IX information: By July 1, 2017, public schools, private schools receiving federal funds, school districts, county offices of education, and charter schools must post on their websites the Title IX coordinator’s contact information; the rights of pupils and the public and the institution’s responsibilities (including specified links and the list in Section 221.8); and how to file and pursue a Title IX complaint, including timelines and links to U.S. Department of Education resources. [5]

- Public access to information via libraries: Union high school districts may establish public libraries for the dissemination of knowledge, and such libraries must be “forever free” to district inhabitants and nonresident taxpayers, subject to library rules. [2]

question: What does Title 1 say about publication or transparency of education information?
answer:
Title 1 includes several provisions related to publication and transparency:

- Title IX transparency online: Public schools, districts, county offices of education, charter schools, and private schools receiving federal funds must prominently post on their websites the Title IX coordinator’s contact information, the rights and responsibilities under Title IX (including links and the list in Section 221.8), and how to file a Title IX complaint with required explanations and links [5].

- County publications to the State Board: The State Board of Education sets definitions for “publications,” and each county superintendent must transmit a copy of any publication they make to the State Board. - Financial transparency and accountability: Title 1 establishes a program of financial and compliance audits for school districts and county offices of education to promote accountability over public educational funding, with oversight by the Controller. Compliance audits verify that funds are spent as required by law, including consistency with local control and accountability plans [4].

- Public access to information resources: Union high school districts may establish public libraries for disseminating knowledge, and such libraries are “forever free” to inhabitants and nonresident taxpayers, subject to library rules [2].

- Library content governance: County boards may adopt lists of library materials for certain districts, and school district governing boards may exclude from schools and school libraries materials of a sectarian, partisan, or denominational character [6].

question: What legal constraints does Title 1 place on education authorities?
answer:
From the provided excerpts of Title 1, the following legal constraints apply to education authorities:

- Title IX website transparency: Public schools, school districts, county offices of education, charter schools, and private schools receiving federal funds must post on their websites (1) the Title IX coordinator’s contact information, (2) the rights of pupils/the public and the institution’s responsibilities under Title IX (with links to CDE’s Office for Equal Opportunity and the U.S. Department of Education OCR, and the list of rights in Section 221.8), and (3) how to file a Title IX complaint, including the statute of limitations and how investigations proceed, with links to OCR resources [2].

- Charter school facilities use and title restrictions: When title to charter school project facilities is held by certain authorized entities, the chain of title must include (1) a restrictive covenant limiting use to public school purposes as authorized by the California Constitution and statute, and (2) a remainder interest to the local school district (or the board if the district disclaims) that is triggered when the facility is no longer needed for charter purposes and then handled under Section 17078.62(b)(2)–(6). The board may adopt regulations to implement these rules. A school district may also elect to include charter facilities in a general facilities application; in that case the project is outside the charter article and must comply with the general chapter like any noncharter project [4].

- Consistency with federal law in program administration: The State Department of Education must promulgate rules and regulations necessary to administer the chapter at issue in a manner consistent with 42 U.S.C. § 1766 and related federal regulations, including setting eligibility requirements [5].

- Required dispute-resolution process in early education contracts: The department must provide an internal appeal procedure to resolve disputes with contracting agencies providing preschool services under Section 8233, including disputes over contract terms or findings from fiscal/programmatic reviews (such as error rate notifications). Contracting agencies have the right to appeal those findings under the department’s internal procedure [6].

- Prohibition on unauthorized academic credentials: It is a misdemeanor for any person—including a public board, agency, or entity—to prepare, manufacture, print, or offer to do so, for compensation, any document purporting to be a degree or diploma without written authorization from the school authority [1].

question: What legal constraints does Title 1 place on education authorities?
answer:
Based on the provided Title 1 excerpts, the following legal constraints apply to education authorities (e.g., school districts, county offices of education, charter schools, and the California Department of Education):

- Prohibited creation of degrees/diplomas without authorization: No person—including a public board, agency, or entity—may prepare, manufacture, print, or offer to do so for a fee any document purporting to be a degree or diploma without written authorization from the school authority; violation is a misdemeanor. Definitions of “person,” “prepare,” “degree,” and “diploma” apply. [1]

- Title IX website disclosures: Public schools, private schools receiving federal funds and subject to Title IX, school districts, county offices of education, and charter schools must post on their websites: (1) Title IX coordinator contact information; (2) rights/responsibilities under Title IX, including links to CDE’s Office for Equal Opportunity and the U.S. Department of Education OCR, and the list of rights in Section 221.8; and (3) how to file a Title IX complaint, including statute of limitations, investigation process, and relevant OCR links. [2]

- Charter school facilities—use and reversion: Title to charter school project facilities held by authorized entities must include in the chain of title: (i) a restrictive covenant limiting use to public school purposes authorized by the California Constitution and statute; and (ii) a remainder interest to the school district (or to the State Allocation Board if the district disclaims) that is triggered when the facility is no longer needed for charter school purposes, subject to specified procedures. Districts may transfer title to certain entities upon request where the district had previously agreed to hold title, on mutually agreed terms. If a district includes charter facilities in a general facilities application (instead of the charter-specific article), the project must comply with the general chapter like any noncharter project. [4]

- Compliance with federal standards in certain programs: The State Department of Education must promulgate rules and regulations necessary to administer the chapter governing adult day care services in a manner consistent with 42 U.S.C. § 1766 and applicable federal regulations, including eligibility requirements. [5]

- Administrative review in early education: The Department must provide an internal appeal procedure for disputes with contracting agencies providing preschool services under Section 8233 regarding contract interpretation or findings from fiscal/programmatic reviews (including error rate notifications). Contracting agencies have the right to appeal such findings pursuant to that procedure. [6]

question: How does Article IX’s education mandate align with Title 1 administrative duties?
answer:
- Article IX sets the purpose and statewide leadership. It declares that the Legislature must “encourage by all suitable means the promotion of intellectual, scientific, moral, and agricultural improvement,” and it establishes the Superintendent of Public Instruction and senior deputies to carry out education duties. [1]

- Title 1 implements that mandate through concrete administrative obligations:
  - Equity compliance: Schools, districts, county offices of education, and charters must post Title IX coordinator information, rights, and complaint procedures on their websites, operationalizing nondiscrimination as part of access to education. [4]
  - Program administration and rulemaking: The State Department of Education must promulgate rules and regulations necessary to administer specified programs consistent with federal law, reflecting the executive implementation role of the education leadership established in Article IX. [5][1]
  - Conditions on specialized schooling: Certain large districts and affiliated charters may maintain single‑gender schools or classes only if they adopt policies ensuring compliance with Title IX regulations, tying local program design to statewide equity standards. [6]

- Governance framework: Article IX also sets voter‑approval requirements for changes to local boards of education in specified circumstances, structuring the local bodies that implement Title 1 duties. [2]

In short, Article IX provides the constitutional “why” and “who” (state purpose and leadership), while Title 1 supplies the “how” (specific administrative duties and compliance mechanisms) to advance the constitution’s education mandate. [1][4][5][6]

question: What constitutional principles support Title 1 governance provisions?
answer:
Key constitutional principles that support (and frame) governance provisions in Education Code Title 1 include:

- Local home-rule and charter authority for cities: City charters may “make and enforce all ordinances and regulations in respect to municipal affairs,” and, as to municipal affairs, charter provisions supersede inconsistent laws. Charters may also provide plenary authority over how municipal officers are elected or appointed, their terms, removal, compensation, and staffing levels [1].  
- County charter governance framework and powers: County charters must provide for a governing body, set compensation and terms, specify elected officers (e.g., sheriff, district attorney, assessor) and other officers, define powers and duties, prescribe how vacancies are filled, and regulate staffing (assistants, deputies, clerks) and their qualifications and compensation. Once approved, a county charter supersedes general laws, as to matters within the charter’s competence; charter counties have all powers provided by the Constitution or by statute for counties [2][1].  
- State law–charter relationship: In areas where a charter is competent and makes provision, it supersedes general laws; in other matters, general laws apply. This delineates how statewide governance statutes (such as Title 1 provisions on governance processes) operate alongside local charter authority [1][2].  
- Qualification to vote or hold office: The right to vote or hold office may not be conditioned on a property qualification, a baseline constitutional protection that undergirds governance schemes involving elections or officeholding [3].

These principles provide the constitutional backdrop for statutory governance structures set in Title 1 (for example, provisions establishing and structuring governing boards and their procedures) [5].

question: How does constitutional educational purpose connect to statutory oversight mechanisms?
answer:
- Constitutional purpose: The Constitution identifies compelling public interests for public education, including making the most effective use of limited financial resources, maximizing educational opportunities, protecting pupil health and safety, and enhancing parents’ ability to participate in the educational process [3].

- Statutory oversight mechanisms that operationalize those purposes:
  - Transparency and accountability for education funds: Local governing boards must decide Education Protection Account spending in open public sessions; funds may not be used for administrative salaries or costs; annual online accounting is required; and independent annual financial and compliance audits must verify proper disbursement and expenditure. These measures both protect scarce resources and facilitate parent/community participation [1].
  - Policy and fiscal oversight through data and reporting: The interstate education commission is empowered to collect and analyze education data, encourage research, develop financing proposals, formulate policy recommendations, adopt bylaws, and issue annual reports to the Governor and Legislature—tools that support efficient, evidence‑based use of education resources [4][5].
  - Controls on state apportionments and asset disposition: The administering board may set eligibility qualifications for districts to receive apportionments, establish procedures and policies, adopt rules for program administration, and require disposal or transfer of replaced property to ensure the highest return to the state and reduce apportionments—direct fiscal oversight to safeguard limited funds [6].

In short, the Constitution’s stated educational purposes (efficient use of funds, maximizing opportunities, safety, and parent participation) are given effect by statutory mechanisms that ensure transparent decision‑making, public reporting, independent auditing, data‑driven policy guidance, and strict fiscal controls over state education funds and assets [1][3][4][5][6].

question: What similarities and differences exist between constitutional and statutory education governance language?
answer:
Similarities
- Both set up or recognize education governance bodies and assign them roles using mandatory “shall” language. Examples include:
  - Constitution: joint county boards/superintendents “shall be governed by the general statutes,” and the Legislature “shall provide for a system of common schools” with free schools maintained at least six months per year [1]. Voter-approval procedures for board governance changes are prescribed in detail [2].
  - Statutes: the State Allocation Board “shall” establish procedures and adopt rules to administer the School Construction Law; the Commission under the Compact for Education “shall” adopt bylaws and make annual reports to the Governor and Legislature [4], [6].
- Both address structure and operations of governing entities:
  - Constitution addresses who may determine election, qualifications, and terms for county boards of education, and when local charter changes to board governance must go to the electorate [1], [2].
  - Statutes specify internal administrative powers (rulemaking, procedures), reporting duties, and member compensation/reimbursement for certain statewide bodies [4], [6].

Differences
- Level and scope:
  - Constitutional provisions set the overarching framework and constraints: they allocate authority among the Legislature, county/city charters, and the electorate; require elector approval for certain local board changes; and define the Public School System and protect it from being placed under non-system authorities [1], [2]. Article XI also outlines general charter-county governance powers in local government, against which Article IX carves education-specific rules [3], [1].
  - Statutory provisions are programmatic and administrative: they empower specific entities (e.g., State Allocation Board, interstate commission) to adopt procedures, rules, conduct research, and report, and they specify member compensation/reimbursement and funding sources for their work [4], [5], [6].
- Who decides:
  - Constitution: determines when county charters may set board election/qualification/term rules (except for joint county entities governed by general statutes) and when changes require districtwide voter approval, especially where district boundaries extend beyond a charter city [1], [2].
  - Statutes: delegate operational authority to boards/commissions to manage programs (school construction administration; interstate policy coordination) via bylaws, rules, and studies, without electorate approval mechanisms [4], [5], [6].
- Democratic checks:
  - Constitution embeds voter-approval requirements for changes to board of education governance in specified boundary situations and mandates separate ballot questions for discrete board-governance issues; failure preserves existing law [2].
  - Statutes emphasize administrative accountability (bylaws, annual reports to governors/legislatures) rather than direct electoral approvals [6].
- Jurisdictional limits and system definition:
  - Constitution defines the Public School System and forbids transferring any part of it to authorities outside the system [1].
  - Statutes do not redefine the system’s jurisdiction; they implement specific programs within it (e.g., school construction; interstate information-sharing and policy development) [4], [5], [6].
- Specificity on compensation/governance mechanics:

- The Constitution also includes some direct substantive mandates (e.g., minimum annual salaries for certificated employees and the six-month free school requirement), which sit alongside governance framework provisions [1]. question: What similarities and differences exist between constitutional and statutory education governance language?
answer:
Similarities
- Both use mandatory, structural language to define who governs and how. Examples: “shall be governed by the general statutes” (joint county boards) and voter approval requirements for changing board governance in certain jurisdictions [1][2]; statutory mandates that specified boards “shall” establish procedures, adopt rules, and file bylaws/reports [4][6].
- Both aim at statewide coherence. The Constitution requires a statewide “system of common schools” and keeps all public schools within the Public School System’s jurisdiction [1], while statutes create coordinating bodies and processes (e.g., the Compact for Education commission) to develop policy and share information across jurisdictions [5][6].

Differences
- Level and scope: Constitutional text sets foundational mandates and structural limits (e.g., free schools at least six months; scope of the Public School System and non-transfer from it; baseline teacher salary; who may set county board election/term rules; voter approval for certain board changes) [1][2]. Statutes implement operational details (e.g., State Allocation Board rulemaking, procedures, reimbursement; interstate commission bylaws, research, financing proposals, and reporting) [4][6].
- Who decides and accountability: The Constitution places key governance changes with voters and delimits charter authority over education boards [1][2]. Statutes vest decisionmaking in administrative bodies (boards/commissions) subject to law, with internal governance (bylaws) and reporting to executives/legislatures rather than direct voter approval [4][6].
- Charter interplay and hierarchy: The Constitution both authorizes county charters to address county boards of education and restricts them (e.g., joint county boards governed by general statutes; elector approval for certain changes) [1][2]. Article XI also shows county charters operate alongside and are subject to statutes for required functions and district apportionment [3]. Statutes, by contrast, directly confer powers/duties on state-level bodies (e.g., State Allocation Board) without relying on local charter instruments [4].
- Specificity and discretion: Constitutional provisions are categorical and structural (“shall provide,” “shall not be governed”) [1][2]; statutory provisions are more granular and often include delegated discretion (“as it deems necessary,” “may make such additional reports”) in administering programs and policy development [4][6].
